title: Irreducibility
body:
A non-constant $f \in F[x]$ is **irreducible over $F$** when it cannot be written as a product of
two polynomials of lower degree with coefficients in $F$. It is the [[Polynomial Ring]] version of
a [[Prime Number]], and it plays the identical role: irreducibles are the atoms, and factorisation
into them is unique up to constants.

**"Over $F$" is not decoration.** Irreducibility is a property of the polynomial *and* the field,
and the same polynomial changes status as the field grows:

| $x^2 + 1$ | over | |
|---|---|---|
| irreducible | $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{R}$ | no real root |
| reducible | $\mathbb{C}$ | $(x-i)(x+i)$ |
| reducible | $\mathbb{Z}_2$ | $x^2+1 = (x+1)^2$, since $2 = 0$ |

$x^2 - 2$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ and splits over $\mathbb{R}$. Every question in this
section is really "which field are we standing in", and adjoining a root of an irreducible is
precisely how you move; see [[Field Extension]].

## Tests

**Degree 2 or 3: a factorisation must include a linear factor, so it is reducible if and only if
it has a root in $F$.** That is the only test most exercises need, and it is the factor theorem
in [[Polynomial Ring]] doing the work. It **fails from degree 4 up**:
$x^4 + 2x^2 + 1 = (x^2+1)^2$ has no rational root and is still reducible. Getting that wrong is
the standard trap.

**Rational root theorem.** A rational root $p/q$ in lowest terms of an integer polynomial has
$p \mid a_0$ and $q \mid a_n$. Finite list, check it.

**Eisenstein's criterion.** If some prime $p$ divides every coefficient except the leading one,
and $p^2 \nmid a_0$, then $f$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.

```
x⁵ + 6x³ + 12x + 18,  take p = 3
    3 | 6, 12, 18      every non-leading coefficient
    3 ∤ 1              the leading one
    9 ∤ 18             the constant, not twice over
    -> irreducible over Q
```

It is a sufficient condition only: failing Eisenstein proves nothing. A substitution such as
$x \mapsto x+1$ sometimes makes it apply where it did not, which is how $1 + x + \cdots + x^{p-1}$
is handled.

**Reduction mod $p$.** If $f$ stays the same degree and is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ for
some prime, it is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$. Useful because $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is finite, so the
check is a search rather than an argument.

## Why the course cares

$F[x]/(f)$ is a [[Field]] exactly when $f$ is irreducible, mirroring "$\mathbb{Z}_n$ is a field
exactly when $n$ is prime" in [[Modular Arithmetic]]. A reducible $f = gh$ gives $[g][h] = [0]$
with neither factor zero, a zero divisor, and a [[Ring]] with those is no field.

So irreducibility is the switch that turns a quotient into a field, which makes it the
gatekeeper for the entire rest of the course. $\mathbb{C}$ exists because $x^2+1$ is irreducible
over $\mathbb{R}$, and $GF(2^8)$ exists because AES picked an irreducible degree-8 polynomial over
$\mathbb{Z}_2$ to reduce by; see [[Finite Field]].
